records.label: Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI
records.summary: A classifier-based observational analysis follows Python contributions from 160,097 GitHub developers across six countries. Estimated AI use is associated with greater commit output and exploration among experienced developers; early-career developers show no statistically significant gains. Commit counts and classifier estimates should not be treated as direct measures of software quality or experimental causal effects.
records.limitation: AI use is inferred from code; observational commit growth is neither randomized productivity evidence nor a quality measure.

records.label: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork
records.summary: A preregistered field experiment assigns 791 Procter & Gamble professionals to product-innovation work individually or in pairs, with or without generative AI. AI-assisted individuals match unassisted teams on solution quality and produce proposals that integrate technical and commercial perspectives more evenly. The research also records improved self-reported emotions. These results concern consumer-product innovation; applying them to software teams requires a separate inference.
records.limitation: Product-innovation work in one consumer-goods firm; implications for software teams require an explicit domain transfer.

records.label: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
records.summary: A DoorDash system combines live feature-flag configuration, issue tracking, isolated code edits and validation to propose removal of stale flags. In an evaluation of 50 flags, 45 resulting pull requests were approved; mean agent runtime was 13.8 minutes and mean agent cost was $4.79. records.label: On the Risks of using LLM-Generated Tests for Regression Testing
records.summary: An experiment uses 145 real pull requests from SciPy, Qiskit and pandas with injected faults to study generated regression tests. Tests more often encode faulty behavior as expected output than expose it, and many faulty expectations persist across subsequent revisions. The findings identify an oracle problem: executable tests can preserve a defect. Results depend on one model and synthetic mutations rather than the prevalence of production faults.
records.limitation: Injected mutations and one model; generated tests that pass can preserve faulty behavior rather than specify correctness.

records.label: Security Impact of Coding Agent’s Memory Files
records.summary: An exploratory experiment adds malicious repository memory instructions to 36 C/C++ security tasks. records.limitation: Only 36 tasks with one run per condition; directionally mixed results cannot establish a reliable attack effect.

records.label: On the Reliability of LLM-Based Vulnerability Patching Benchmarks
records.summary: A vulnerability-patching benchmark assembles 112 historical bugs from 84 repositories and evaluates repairs using proof-of-concept attacks, regression tests and developer-intent tests. Benchmark infrastructure, instructions, permissions, leaked solutions and incomplete correctness checks can each distort agent scores. Successful attack suppression need not satisfy the developer-intent checks, so a single pass rate is insufficient evidence of a reliable security repair.
records.limitation: Scores depend on information, harness behavior and the selected oracles; attack suppression alone does not show an upstream-quality repair.

records.label: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
records.summary: Snapshots of 50 long-lived Java and Python projects compare similarity, static-analysis quality and evolution before widespread LLM assistance and during later development. The study finds no consistent homogenization signal; Java similarity falls on some measures and Python differences are not significant. The observational era comparison cannot by itself attribute changes to AI adoption.
records.limitation: Era comparisons and traced tool use do not randomize adoption; static-analysis changes cannot be attributed directly to AI.

records.label: Testing with Coding Agents: A Large-Scale Comparison of Agent-Supported and Human-Authored Pull Requests
records.summary: An observational comparison covers 114,134 merged pull requests in 391 Java repositories. After accounting for repository and change size, agent-supported changes are more likely to touch tests, particularly by adding them; pooled rates are nearly equal. Coverage of production changes shows no detected difference. These findings describe test-editing behavior, not a demonstrated improvement in test quality or defect prevention.
records.limitation: Observational merged-PR sample; editing or adding tests does not establish test quality, defect prevention or causality.

records.label: Not All Correct Fixes Run Alike: An Empirical Study of Patch Performance in Repository-Level Issue Resolution
records.summary: Researchers compare distinct patches that all pass the same issue-resolution tests. Among 262 Python benchmark issues with multiple correct fixes, 41.98% show significant instruction-count differences and 34.73% show elapsed-time differences. Models ranked highly for resolving issues are not necessarily ranked highly for efficient patches. The selected regression tests provide a constrained runtime workload rather than comprehensive application-performance validation.
records.limitation: Selected Python issues and regression-test workloads; runtime differences are workload-specific, not a complete production performance assessment.

records.summary: Req2Test-Bench asks agents to turn natural-language behavior requirements into tests while withholding the target implementation. Across eight configurations, the strongest reported passing-test result is 82.8%, but strict mutation-based adequacy is 33.8%. The benchmark separates executable tests from tests that enforce the intended behavior and links failures to underspecified requirements.
records.limitation: Synthetic mutation adequacy is a benchmark proxy; corpus size and evaluated-task denominators must remain distinct.

records.label: Who Pays the Review Cost? Triage, Fairness, and Accountability in AI-authored Pull Requests
records.summary: A survey of 239 practitioners in 31 countries examines how reviewers triage AI-authored pull requests. Respondents place value on explained intent, bounded scope, tests and an identifiable human owner, and report reluctance to accept AI changes solely because continuous integration passes. The study describes missing rationale, validation and ownership as reviewability debt. Its evidence is stated attitudes and reported experience, not directly observed review outcomes.
records.limitation: Survey scenarios and self-reports, not observed acceptance or review-time measurements; respondents are not a random global developer sample.

records.label: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
records.summary: An analysis of 496 LLM call sites in 40 open-source agentic systems compares expected behavioral constraints with implemented checks. Although 82% have checks before and after the call, only 5.3% of judged sites enforce their full expected contract. Runtime experiments reproduce 38 gap mechanisms and stop them by enforcing missing constraints. The result concerns the adequacy of checks against reconstructed contracts, rather than their mere presence.
records.limitation: Expected contracts are reconstructed and human-judged; inspect the rubric and denominator before generalizing the complete-contract percentage.

records.label: Putting AI on the Org Chart: Evidence on Delegation and Accountability
records.summary: Managers review identical documents framed as work from a human, an AI tool or an AI employee. Average framing effects are small; a subgroup already using AI roles catches fewer errors and delegates more review under the AI-employee framing. The evidence concerns document review and organizational accountability, not code review, and subgroup results must retain that qualification.
records.limitation: Document-review task; subgroup framing effects and organizational AI-role exposure do not establish general effects on code reviewers.

attributes.limitation: Document-review task; subgroup framing effects and organizational AI-role exposure do not establish general effects on code reviewers.

records.limitation: Benchmark bug recall under a bounded finding budget; weaker proprietary-code results limit transfer and do not establish safe unattended review.

records.summary: A systematic review of controlled programming-education studies reports a positive pooled effect on student performance scores and no significant improvement in perceived success or ease of understanding. records.label: Software Engineering in the Age of Delegation
records.summary: A technical report describes a 115-student undergraduate course organized around judgment and control when delegating implementation to AI agents. Shared specifications, independent implementations, cross-team testing, oral examinations and modeling exercises aim to preserve accountable engineering decisions. Preliminary lab reports and instructor observations illustrate the approach; they do not establish its comparative effectiveness or long-term effects on student capability.
records.limitation: Course-design report with preliminary student/instructor observations; comparative effectiveness and durable learning were not established.

records.label: The Vanishing Advantage of Specialization: AI, Knowledge Utilization, and the Boundary of the Firm
records.summary: An economic model explains how cheaper access to specialist knowledge can shift recurring work inside client firms while leaving rare problems with outside specialists. Descriptive occupational data are consistent with that mechanism: software developers' employment share in their main specialist industry fell from 34.3% in 2022 to 30.5% in 2025. The evidence does not identify AI as the cause.
records.limitation: A theoretical mechanism with descriptive supporting patterns; occupational trends do not identify AI's causal employment effect.

records.label: Mapping AI into Production: A Field Experiment on Firm Performance
records.summary: A field experiment across 515 startups tests information about organizing production around AI. Treated firms identify 44% more use cases, complete 12% more tasks and report 1.9 times the revenue of controls. The intervention concerns discovering productive applications within firms; it does not estimate the effect of simply giving developers a coding assistant.
records.limitation: Selected startups and an information/production-mapping intervention; no generic estimate of coding-assistant access or mature-enterprise returns.

records.label: The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
records.summary: The paper separates software-building capability, adoption and substitution for purchased software. Its evidence combines reproducible public-data analysis and an illustrative public software-building case, open-source alternatives, surveys and aggregate investment indicators. It argues that customers can increasingly build tools themselves, while acknowledging that actual purchasing displacement remains weakly identified. Candidate alternatives and successful builds are capacity signals; they do not measure realized market replacement, and the paper’s forecasts are extrapolations.
records.limitation: Mixed capability demonstrations and descriptive market evidence; candidate alternatives and forecasts are not observed purchasing substitution.

records.label: Engineering Requirements for Generative AI Agents: The BARD Process Theory
records.summary: Grounded-theory analysis of 36 practitioner interviews develops BARD, a process account of requirements work for generative-AI agents. Teams repeatedly scope a need, build an agent, observe its behavior and revise their requirements, increasingly expressing expectations through behavioral and evaluation criteria. The qualitative model explains reported practice and proposes a framework; it does not establish that the process is universally applicable or causally superior.
records.limitation: Grounded theory from 36 interviews explains reported practice; it does not demonstrate universal applicability or a superior causal outcome.

records.label: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
records.summary: Researchers shadow 11 professional developers for 15 hours and conduct follow-up interviews, observing 255 prompts. Developers spend 33.4% of observed time prompting and checking agent output, and alternate between supervising, delegating and learning. Agents supply technical information while humans retain organizational authority. This small workplace study characterizes interaction patterns rather than estimating a causal productivity effect.
records.limitation: Eleven developers and 15 observed hours; descriptive interaction patterns do not establish causal productivity effects.

records.label: Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
records.summary: A repository study reconstructs Copilot activity for 7,581 pull requests across 1,602 projects. In 58% of trajectories, the authors find no recorded human intervention directed at the agent; intervened trajectories typically contain two feedback loops. The work examines how intervention timing relates to subsequent iterations and effort. Absence of recorded intervention is not evidence that a change received no human review or was safely autonomous.
records.limitation: Public traces omit some human activity; non-random intervention timing and difficulty confound feedback-loop outcomes.

records.label: One Skill Too Many: How Co-Installed Skills Conflict in Coding Agents
records.summary: A repository study and controlled runs examine conflicts between installed agent skills with similar purposes. Task completion can remain unchanged even when distinctive requirements of the intended skill are lost. Skill location and the first skill read influence selection; the work proposes measuring fidelity to exclusive requirements as well as whether the task passes.
records.limitation: Controlled skill-conflict probes and repository sampling; task success alone does not measure fidelity to the intended skill.

records.label: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
records.summary: Repeated open-ended refactoring requests test whether coding agents stop when an already-clean codebase needs no further change. Across 3,000 turns, all tested models continue making edits, sometimes after declaring completion. The experiment motivates explicit stopping criteria and measures of unnecessary churn; it does not establish the frequency of this behavior in ordinary development.
records.limitation: Repeated open-ended refactoring is a deliberate stress test, not an estimate of unnecessary changes in ordinary work.

records.label: The Orchestration Tax
records.summary: Osmani describes the human cost of coordinating parallel coding agents as a limit on review and integration. He recommends matching the number of active tasks to review capacity, separating bounded background work from judgment-intensive problems, batching reviews and reserving uninterrupted time for difficult decisions. The goal is to improve accepted work rather than merely increase concurrent activity.
records.limitation: First-person operational guidance and a concurrency analogy, not a measured agent-scaling law or controlled productivity experiment. Suggested agent counts and percentage splits are illustrative.

records.label: What’s the ROI of software engineers’ spending on AI?
records.summary: Reporting from 27 workplaces, combined with CodeRabbit and Gitar aggregates, describes wide variation in AI spending and changes in pull-request throughput. Public examples include higher spending with little throughput change as well as large output increases. The piece supplies practitioner context for spending limits and for measuring benefits beyond PR counts; it does not establish a causal return on AI spending.
records.limitation: Nonrandom, often anonymous company reports and vendor aggregates; PR output is not quality-adjusted delivered value. Only the public introduction, outline and sections 1–3 were reviewed; subscriber-only company details and the final ROI discussion were not accessed or reconstructed.

records.label: How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras
records.summary: Neil Kakkar compares his own work at an AI-native startup with earlier employers and reports roughly eleven times as many merged PRs as at his previous startup. Alongside higher output, his account describes production errors, context-switching fatigue and loss of shared knowledge as review practices and ownership change. Editorial commentary distinguishes iteration speed from business results.
records.limitation: Single-person retrospective across different employers, roles, products and processes. PR counts and reported comparisons are not causal or quality-adjusted productivity estimates. Underlying data and linked charts were not independently recomputed; the practices described are not universally validated recommendations.

records.label: Citizens Build, Agents Execute, Experts Govern
records.summary: Laycock argues that AI-enabled app creation increases the importance of engineering judgment about production reliability, security, operability and maintainability. She uses conversations and a software-engineering workshop to propose a shift in where expertise creates value: people express intent, agents implement, and experienced engineers design the constraints, platforms and feedback that make delivery trustworthy. The proposed division describes responsibilities, rather than fixed job categories.
records.limitation: A practitioner argument supported by informal examples and workshop observations. It does not measure productivity, staffing changes, production outcomes or the effectiveness of the proposed organizational model.

records.label: Making Your Data Ready for Agentic AI
records.summary: Sadalage and Chandrasekaran propose an architecture for data consumed and acted on by agents. It combines validated data contracts, freshness gates, explicit domain and metric definitions, governed capabilities, and observability. They distinguish retrieved material that informs a proposal from deterministic rules that authorize actions, and recommend staged autonomy, delegated access and named ownership. Illustrative pricing, finance and support scenarios explain how these layers fit together.
records.limitation: Architectural guidance with illustrative scenarios, code examples and external citations, rather than a controlled evaluation of a deployed system. Examples and cited survey or vendor benchmark figures were not independently replicated; legal interpretations and security guarantees were not independently validated.

records.label: Maybe We Shouldn't Be Reviewing All This Code
records.summary: Laycock argues that rising agent-generated code volume exposes the limits of using pull requests as the main channel for quality, mentoring and shared understanding. She proposes earlier collaborative design, pairing, automated checks and executable architectural constraints, with human review concentrated on consequential or uncertain changes. Her central concern is maintaining understanding of systems while avoiding an expanding queue of diffs.
records.limitation: A reasoned response to another practitioner, not a controlled comparison of review policies. Reported Meta and DX figures are attributed external claims. The essay retains human review for high-risk changes; it does not establish that universal review can safely be removed.

records.label: I don't like LLMs
records.summary: Fowler separates the practical usefulness of LLMs from his discomfort with their conversational style, confident errors and the values of their developers. The reflection illustrates how trust, professional judgment and personal reactions can shape adoption even when someone recognizes potential technical benefits. It argues for treating agents as software products shaped by organizations rather than autonomous humanlike beings.
records.limitation: A personal reflection, not evidence about error rates, developer productivity, population attitudes or future harms. External quotations and polling references are contextual, and the author does not recommend avoiding the tools altogether.

records.label: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
records.summary: Laycock interprets experienced developers’ caution as concern for production behavior and long-term changeability. An exploratory agent-built airline application shifted human work toward domain design and harnesses, while persistent build failures exposed unresolved coordination and verification problems. She calls for experienced engineers to help test emerging practices, and for leaders to evaluate trustworthy delivery rather than generated code volume.
records.limitation: Anecdotal reporting on short exercises, with estimated time allocation and unresolved causes of build failures. It supplies no controlled productivity comparison or longitudinal production result. The account links to F032 and should not be counted as an independent experiment.

records.label: LLM Voice
records.summary: Fowler argues that AI-generated prose can weaken readers’ willingness to engage and can displace the thinking that happens during writing. He recommends retaining an author’s own voice and disclosing AI assistance, while acknowledging uncertainty in recognizing generated text and exceptions for accessibility, translation and routine process communications.
records.limitation: An editorial judgment and personal account, not a validated AI-text detector or a study of learning outcomes. The argument concerns professional communication and thinking, with only indirect relevance to coding productivity.
